Warlock and witch dossier

Project 33 · 22 warlocks from the archive (9 tried, 8 scholar, 5 teacher) and 11 witches (11 tried) · index · repo randomcase/warlock-and-witch-dossier

What the two halves have in common

The warlock archive files three kinds of person under one word: the tried, who were killed for it; the scholars, who did chemistry and medicine before those had names and were called sorcerers for it afterwards; and the teachers, whose traditions remember them as more than human. The witch half has no scholars and no teachers. Every entry is tried. That asymmetry is the finding: the same century that called a man with a laboratory a magus called a woman with a garden a witch, and only one of those words came with a bishop’s mitre at the end.

Three trials appear on both sides — North Berwick 1591 (Fian, Sampson), Salem 1692 (Burroughs, Corey; Bishop, Nurse, Tituba) — which is the second finding: a panic does not sort by sex, it sorts by who is nearest.

Entries

Warlocks

tried · Salem, Massachusetts · 1692
Rev. George Burroughs — A minister, and a former minister of Salem Village itself.

Recited the Lord’s Prayer perfectly on the gallows, which was held to be impossible for a witch. He was hanged anyway.

fate: hanged

tried · Salem Farms · 1692
Giles Corey — A prosperous landowner in his eighties.

Refused to plead, so there was no conviction and no forfeiture. Two days under stones and his sons inherited. The only defeat of the mechanism in this archive.

fate: pressed to death

tried · Bamberg · 1628
Johannes Junius — Burgomaster of Bamberg.

His letter to his daughter survives, written from the cell: the confession was false and extracted, and he said so in writing while he still could.

fate: burned

tried · Trier · 1589
Dietrich Flade — A senior judge, and wealthy.

He grew sceptical of the evidence in front of him and was tried himself. Doubt was survivable only in silence.

fate: executed

tried · Loudun · 1634
Urbain Grandier — A priest with powerful political enemies, including Richelieu.

Convicted on the testimony of possessed nuns. The trial is one of the best-documented in Europe and reads throughout as a factional settling.

fate: burned

tried · North Berwick · 1591
John Fian — A schoolmaster.

Accused of raising the storm that struck James VI’s ship. The king attended the examinations personally and later wrote a book about demonology.

fate: executed

tried · Edinburgh · 1670
Major Thomas Weir — A respected Covenanter officer, seventy years old.

He confessed unprompted to crimes nobody had accused him of. The one case here where the confession preceded the accusation.

fate: strangled and burned

tried · Saint-Domingue · 1758
François Makandal — An enslaved man, a maroon leader, and by every account a genuinely skilled herbalist.

Organised a poisoning campaign against planters. The charge was sorcery; the activity was insurrection, and the colonial court had reason to prefer the first word.

fate: burned

tried · Rome · 1600
Giordano Bruno — A Dominican friar, philosopher and cosmologist.

Held that the stars were suns with worlds of their own. The charges were theological rather than sorcerous, and he is here because the archive filed him here — which is itself the point.

fate: burned

scholar · Persia · 1037
Ibn Sina (Avicenna) — A physician and philosopher.

Wrote the Canon of Medicine, which was a standard text in European universities for roughly six hundred years. Filing him under warlock is a Western taxonomy applied to a man who had a different job.

fate: died of illness, at court

scholar · Rayy and Baghdad · 925
Al-Razi (Rhazes) — A physician and chemist.

First clear clinical distinction between smallpox and measles, and an early sceptic of alchemy as transmutation while doing the chemistry anyway.

fate: died blind, in poverty

scholar · Kufa · 815
Jabir ibn Hayyan (Geber) — A chemist, or a corpus of chemists writing under one name.

The word alchemy carries an Arabic article on the front of it because of this tradition. Distillation, crystallisation and classification of substances are all in the corpus.

fate: unknown

scholar · Oxford and Paris · 1292
Roger Bacon — A Franciscan friar and natural philosopher.

Argued for experiment and mathematics against argument from authority. Later legend made him a magician; he was a monk with a lens.

fate: died a friar

scholar · Cologne · 1280
Albertus Magnus — A Dominican friar, Aquinas’s teacher.

Catalogued plants and minerals systematically. He is a SAINT, and he is in a warlock archive, and both of those are true at once.

fate: died a bishop, later canonised

scholar · Mortlake · 1609
John Dee — Mathematician, navigator, and Elizabeth I’s astrologer.

Assembled the largest library in England and advised on navigation for the northern voyages. Also spent years attempting to speak with angels through Edward Kelley, and both halves are him.

fate: died poor

scholar · Basel and Salzburg · 1541
Paracelsus — A physician.

"The dose makes the poison" is his, and it is the founding sentence of toxicology. He also burned Avicenna’s books in public, which tells you something about the temperament.

fate: died at forty-seven

teacher · China, from South India · 536
Bodhidharma — The traditional founder of Chan Buddhism.

Chan becomes Zen. He is a religious founder for hundreds of millions of people and appears here because a Western category was laid over him from outside.

fate: tradition disputes it

teacher · Tibet · 800
Padmasambhava — The figure credited with establishing Buddhism in Tibet.

Called Guru Rinpoche by millions of living practitioners. The "sorcery" is a tradition of tantric practice described by people outside it.

fate: tradition says he did not die

teacher · Sichuan · 156
Zhang Daoling — Founder of the Way of the Celestial Masters.

The first organised Daoist church. A religious institution, filed under sorcery by a taxonomy that had no other box for it.

fate: tradition says he ascended

teacher · Tibet · 1135
Milarepa — Tibet’s most celebrated poet and yogi.

His life story opens with him using sorcery for revenge and spends the rest of itself on the consequences. The tradition itself treats the magic as the sin.

fate: poisoned, by tradition

teacher · Heian Japan · 1005
Abe no Seimei — An onmyōji — a court diviner and calendar official.

A civil servant. Onmyōdō was a government bureau handling the calendar, timekeeping and divination, and he ran it well enough to be remembered for a thousand years.

fate: died at eighty-four, honoured

scholar · Jin China · 343
Ge Hong — A Daoist writer and physician.

The Baopuzi contains the earliest known description of smallpox symptoms and practical chemistry alongside the immortality material. Both are in the same book by the same person.

fate: died in retirement

Witches

tried · Kilkenny · 1324
Alice Kyteler — A four-times-widowed moneylender.

The first recorded witchcraft trial in Ireland was about an inheritance. The heresy charge arrived after the stepchildren’s complaint, not before it.

fate: fled; her servant Petronilla was burned in her place

tried · Rouen · 1431
Joan of Arc — A peasant who led an army at seventeen.

Convicted for heresy and for wearing men’s clothes, not for sorcery as such. The dossier keeps her because every later witch trial borrowed the shape of hers.

fate: burned; verdict annulled 1456; canonised 1920

tried · North Berwick · 1591
Agnes Sampson — A midwife and healer, the “wise wife of Keith”.

Examined by James VI in person. The same trial as John Fian on the warlock side — one storm, two archives.

fate: strangled and burned

tried · Fulda · 1603
Merga Bien — A wealthy heiress.

Her pregnancy after fourteen childless years was entered as evidence. Fulda’s prince-abbot ran roughly two hundred and fifty such cases in three years.

fate: burned, pregnant

tried · Leonberg · 1620
Katharina Kepler — The astronomer’s mother.

Johannes Kepler dropped his work and argued the defence himself, for six years. She was shown the instruments of torture and still did not confess. Acquitted — the rare entry that ends that way.

fate: released after fourteen months; died six months later

tried · Auldearn · 1662
Isobel Gowdie — A cottar’s wife.

Four confessions, apparently unforced, full of verse — the fullest first-person account of what a witch was supposed to do. No record says what became of her.

fate: unrecorded

tried · Stockholm · 1676
Malin Matsdotter — A Finnish-born widow.

Denounced by her own daughters. Sweden burned the confessed after strangling them; she refused to confess and so was burned alive, the only one in that panic who was.

fate: burned alive

tried · Salem Village · 1692
Tituba — An enslaved woman in the Parris household.

The first to confess, and her confession supplied the script the rest of Salem then followed. She outlived the panic because confessors were not hanged.

fate: jailed thirteen months; sold to pay her jail fees

tried · Salem · 1692
Bridget Bishop — A tavern-keeper who wore a red bodice.

The evidence included the bodice, poppets in a cellar wall, and being disliked. Same year and same court as Burroughs and Corey on the other side.

fate: hanged, the first

tried · Salem · 1692
Rebecca Nurse — A seventy-one-year-old church member.

The jury acquitted her. The judge sent them back. That is the whole entry.

fate: hanged, after a not-guilty verdict was reversed

tried · Glarus · 1782
Anna Göldi — A maidservant.

The last person executed for witchcraft in Europe, by a Protestant canton, in the decade of the American Revolution. The exoneration came two hundred and twenty-six years later.

fate: beheaded; exonerated 2008

Method

Warlock entries are read verbatim from the JSON files; the witch entries live in session-index.mjs until a templates-witch/ directory exists, at which point the script should read that instead. Dates are the year of trial or death. “Fate” is the record’s last word, not a judgement.
